issues.issue: The Application is "incorporated herein by reference" and warranted to be "complete, accurate and truthful", but neither the standard of completeness nor the effect of incorporation on the operative terms is specified. A court could be asked what the incorporated Application actually adds to the contract.

Breach of this warranty is a just-cause ground under provision 14.1(E) ("any breach of Employee's warranties"), but the entire-agreement clause 24.1 says the Contract supersedes all previous understandings, leaving the Application's status arguable.

The first "Contract Year" is defined as a thirteen-month period (Dec. 16, 2010 - Jan. 15, 2012) while all others are twelve months, so per-Contract-Year amounts are unevenly measured. A court could be asked how that oversized first year is counted.

The irregular first Contract Year interacts awkwardly with provision 14.2's liquidated damages of $750,000 "per Contract Year, pro rated, for the then-unexpired Term", making the pro-ration for the first year uncertain. That is a computation question spanning two provisions.

The obligation is only to "meet to discuss" and the University "in its sole discretion — may consider" an extension, which is an agreement to agree with no ascertainable standard. A court could be asked whether it creates any enforceable duty at all.

Salary is stated to be "compensation for his services to the University and satisfactory performance of the terms and conditions of this Contract", which could be read as conditioning salary on satisfactory performance. "Satisfactory" is undefined and unmeasured.

Benefits are defined by reference to the Staff Handbook, an external document that can change, so the content of the promised benefits is not fixed by the instrument. A court could be asked which version governs.

Provision 24.2(d) reserves the University's right to modify benefits unilaterally, and provision 11.1 displaces Handbook rules for vacation, so the extent to which the Handbook actually governs is contestable.
The club is only a "mutually agreed upon golf or country club", leaving the essential term to future agreement with no fallback if the parties disagree. That is a classic agreement-to-agree gap.

Forfeiture turns on whether "the University reasonably determines" non-compliance, a self-judging standard qualified only by reasonableness. A court could be asked how much deference that determination gets.

The tickets are provided "at no cost" yet "all of which shall be used for his official responsibilities", a restriction whose boundary (what counts as official use of a season ticket) is undefined. A court could be asked whether personal use breaches it.

Reimbursement is limited to "appropriate" travel and out-of-pocket expenses "reasonably incurred", two undefined qualifiers, and the enumerated NCAA recruiting expenses sit against an open "including but not limited to". The reach of the catch-all is contestable.

The bonus structure is internally muddled: subparagraph A promises "the greatest of" three alternatives, two of which are the identical $100,000, the second bullet is unlabelled, and the items are joined by both "or" and "and". Whether A, B and C are cumulative or alternative is genuinely uncertain.

The $150,000 is payable "while the Employee is representing the University as Head Football Coach" in two installments, but the parenthetical "(by January 1, 2012 for the first Contract Year)" does not say whether both installments or only the second are due then. The payment mechanics for the irregular first Contract Year are ambiguous.

The paragraph declares itself to relate to "this provision 3.8" although it appears within the 3.9 block, so the matters to which the publicity consent attaches are misidentified. A court could be asked which provision the consent actually covers.

"Full time, attention and energies" and the duty to "take every precaution" to ensure staff compliance are open-ended standards with no measurable boundary. A court could be asked what conduct falls short of them.

The full-time-and-attention duty is expressly "subject to any exceptions hereinafter expressly described", yet provision 10.1 permits outside contracting for separate compensation, so the interaction of the two is arguable.

The nine enumerated duties end with "(9) such other duties as assigned from time to time by the University's Director of Athletics", a catch-all whose reach against the specific list is undefined. Duties such as "maintaining a good working relationship with the University community" are also unmeasurable.
Termination is authorised only for "significant or repetitive violations" of NCAA Rules, neither adjective being defined. A court could be asked which violations cross that line.

This provision permits termination only for significant or repetitive NCAA violations, while provision 14.1(B) makes "any violation of NCAA Rules" just cause for immediate termination; the opening "[w]ithout limiting any other provision" only partly reconciles them.

The Employee may offer input on listed matters "and other matters pertaining to the operation of the Team", a general phrase appended to a specific list whose reach is uncertain. Its practical effect is limited because final decisions rest with the Director of Athletics.

The Employee must appear "at such times and places as the University may reasonably require", with "reasonably" the only limit on an otherwise unlimited demand. A court could be asked where that limit lies.

The bar on appearing on "any competing shows or programs" does not define what competes with the Programs, and "such reasonable services as may be requested" is likewise open-ended. Both terms could be read broadly or narrowly.

As with provision 3.9, the parenthetical "(by January 1, 2012 for the first Contract Year)" does not make clear whether one or both installments of the $350,000 fall due on that date. The first Contract Year's payment schedule is therefore uncertain.

The provision breaks off mid-sentence ("the University shall have the right (and shall"), so the scope of the publicity rights granted cannot be read from its own text. Whatever right it confers has to be supplied from elsewhere.
Its content can only be reconstructed from the parallel grant in the provision 3.9 publicity paragraph, and the two may not have identical scope. A court would have to harmonise them.

The text begins mid-sentence ("form acceptable to the University; naming the University as an additional insured"), so the insurance and camp obligations it qualifies are absent from the provision. Its subject cannot be identified from the words given.

The conditions attach to a football-camp right whose granting language does not appear in the instrument, leaving provisions 9.2 to 9.5 to supply a predicate that is missing. A court would have to reconstruct the camp arrangement from the surrounding provisions.

The Employee "shall not unreasonably withhold consent when reasonable alternative facilities are offered", leaving both the reasonableness of alternatives and the consequences of a withheld consent open. The ten-month consultation deadline also has no stated sanction.

The first sentence prohibits public use of the Employee's publicity rights without approval, and the next says "[w]ithout limiting the foregoing, the Employee shall be permitted to contract independently" subject to the same approval; a prohibition and a permission are joined by a non-limiting connector. Whether outside endorsement contracting is barred or merely conditioned is genuinely uncertain.

The clause makes changes in NCAA, conference and University rules "automatically apply to this Contract without the necessity of a written modification", which cannot be squared with provision 24.1's requirement that the Contract not be "amended or modified in any manner, except by an instrument in writing signed by both of the parties".

The heading "Employee Retains all Revenues" is contradicted by the body, which subjects retention to limitations in the Contract and in University, conference and NCAA rules. Provision 21.1 says captions do not control, but the mismatch still invites argument about the residual entitlement.

"Usurp any corporate opportunities of the University" and "any activity causing a conflict of interest" are both undefined and, applied to a university athletics department, have no settled boundary. A court could be asked what falls inside them.

The parenthetical example — that unused vacation may not be retained "(for example during a renewal term of this Contract, if any)" — describes retention across a renewal, which is not the same thing as retention after expiration or termination. The illustration does not fit the rule it illustrates.

The clause displaces "anything contained herein or in University rules, regulations or policies to the contrary" for vacation, while provision 3.2 makes Staff Handbook benefits generally applicable; the override is expressly limited to vacation, so the two are reconcilable.

The Employee has "authority to select, hire, establish the salaries of, and dismiss" staff but "all subject to the prior approval" of the Director of Athletics, so the authority granted may be no authority at all. A court could be asked whether any independent power survives the proviso.
A "dual reporting relationship" to both the Head Coach and the Director of Athletics is created without saying whose direction prevails in a conflict. The term is undefined.

The University's budget "shall not be less than" $1,900,000 per Contract Year while the Employee must keep costs "within the University's allotted budget", which may be a different, later-set figure. Whether the allotted budget is fixed at the floor or set unilaterally is uncertain.

The whole operation of the clause turns on "just cause", a term the contract defines only partly and "in addition to its normally understood meaning in employment contracts", leaving an undefined residue. Whether particular conduct is just cause is exactly the kind of question a court must decide.

The clause opens "[n]otwithstanding any other provisions hereof" and relieves the University of "all further obligations", which sits directly against provision 14.2's guaranteed liquidated damages for termination without just cause; the characterisation of a given termination determines which provision governs.

Subparagraph (F) makes just cause, "as determined by the University", any conduct "seriously prejudicial to the best interests of the University" or that "brings the University into disrepute" — self-judging and unbounded language. Whether the University's own determination is conclusive, and what counts as seriously prejudicial, are live construction questions.

Subparagraph (A) specifically requires "conviction of a violation of a criminal statute", yet the catch-alls in (F) and (G) would allow termination for uncharged or unproven conduct, so the specific enumeration is arguably swallowed by the general. That is a classic expressio unius / ejusdem generis tension.

Liquidated damages are "in, and only in, the amount of Seven Hundred Fifty Thousand Dollars ($750,000) per Contract Year, pro rated, for the then-unexpired Term", but the pro-ration base is unstated and the first Contract Year is thirteen months. The computation is contestable on its face.

The provision applies only "[i]f, but only if" the University terminates without just cause, so it stands or falls on provision 14.1's just-cause definition; the two provisions have to be read together to know which applies.

Payment "as if salary, in equal monthly installments in the manner described in provision 3.1" must be reconciled with provision 14.1's statement that on just-cause termination the University is relieved of all further obligations, but the two address different terminations.

The offset turns on the Employee's "compensation, from any source" in "other employment", an undefined phrase that could capture unrelated or self-employment income. "Reasonable and diligent efforts" is likewise unmeasured.

A mitigation and offset duty is difficult to square with provision 14.2's characterisation of the same payment as fixed "liquidated damages" payable "in, and only in" a stated amount. A court could be asked whether the sum is truly liquidated.

The clawback is triggered by an NCAA finding of a violation "of which Employee reasonably should have known and prevented", a standard applied after the fact and without any process specified. Its boundary is uncertain.

Liability is triggered if the Employee "unilaterally resign[s] or otherwise terminate[s] his employment", a phrase broad enough to be argued to reach a constructive or University-provoked departure. The $3,000,000 figure also raises whether the stipulation is a penalty.

The Employee's exposure of $3,000,000 for leaving contrasts with the University's capped $750,000 per year under provision 14.2, an asymmetry that would frame any argument to construe genuine ambiguity against the University as drafter.

The Employee may not "seek, apply for, discuss or negotiate, either directly or indirectly" other employment without consent, with no standard governing when consent may be refused. What counts as indirect discussion is undefined.

Provision 14.10 lists 14.7 among the exceptions to the cessation of University payment obligations, yet 14.7 itself says obligations "terminate immediately" on death subject only to salary through the date of death; the cross-reference is loose but reconcilable.

Disability is defined by an impairment "expected to result in death or that can be expected to last... not less than twelve (12) months", yet termination is "immediate", so the University must act on an expectation rather than an event. Who makes that determination is unstated.

Provision 14.10 preserves obligations "expressly described in provisions ... and 14.8", but 14.8 describes no surviving payment obligation at all — it terminates them; the exception refers to a provision that contains nothing to except.

The list of exceptions — "provisions 14.2, 14.3, 14.4, 14.7, and 14.8" — includes 14.4 (which terminates payments) and 14.8 (which terminates obligations), neither of which creates a surviving University obligation, so the carve-out list does not cohere with the provisions it names.

The restraint runs "commencing on the date the Employee properly delivers notice of such resignation", so if he leaves without proper notice the period has no start date; the geographic reach ("within the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania and/or at any other Big East Conference... member-institution") is also joined by an ambiguous "and/or".

The Contract is said to be "governed by" undefined "principles and precepts and regulations" relating to equal opportunity, an unidentified body of norms. Which principles are incorporated cannot be told from the text.
Provision 22.1 states that the Contract "shall be governed by and construed under the laws of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania", so two provisions each purport to say what governs the Contract.

The parties must "take whatever measures are necessary" and use "best efforts" to keep the Contract confidential, unbounded standards imposed on a public university employment agreement. What measures are "necessary" is not ascertainable from the text.

Confidentiality of the Contract is qualified only by provision 17.3's carve-out for disclosure "required... by law", which leaves open how it operates for a state-related institution subject to public disclosure duties.

"Private information" is defined as anything known by the Employee as a consequence of employment "and not generally known outside the University", a definition with no subject-matter limit and no time limit. Its boundary would have to be construed.

The carve-out is expressed as "[n]otwithstanding anything contained in provision 17.1" only, leaving the separate and broader confidentiality duty in provision 17.2 without any legally-required-disclosure exception. That omission invites an expressio unius argument.

Notice to the Employee may go to "his University address", which ceases to exist on termination — precisely when notices under provisions 14.1 and 14.2 matter most. Effective notice on termination is therefore uncertain.

The Executive Vice Chancellor's decision is "final within the University" and this is the "exclusive internal dispute resolution mechanism", but nothing says whether resort to it is a condition precedent to suit. Whether the procedure is mandatory or permissive is arguable.

The finality language must be read with the immediately following paragraph preserving each party's right to go to court in Allegheny County; "final within the University" is the only thing reconciling them.

The clause says nothing "shall prevent" resort to court yet also says the parties "agree and consent" that jurisdiction and venue "shall be" in Allegheny County, so whether it is permissive or an exclusive forum selection is open. The two halves pull in different directions.

A requirement that all disputes "be treated confidentially by both parties, at all times" cannot fully coexist with the immediately preceding paragraph permitting either party to litigate in open court. The tension is real but marginal.

The clause says "the Contract shall be ineffective only to the extent of such prohibition", conflating severance of the offending provision with ineffectiveness of the Contract. The drafting leaves what is actually severed slightly unclear.

The requirement that the Contract not be "amended or modified in any manner, except by an instrument in writing signed by both of the parties" is contradicted by provision 10.1(B), under which rule changes "shall automatically apply to this Contract without the necessity of a written modification".

The University may modify benefits that are "part of a larger program that is modified for all other employees" and owes no replacement, which could be read to reach the individually negotiated benefits in section 3. The scope of "benefits hereunder" is uncertain.
Read broadly it would let the University withdraw the specific benefits promised in provisions 3.2 to 3.6 without compensation, which is hard to reconcile with those express undertakings.

The opening excuses a party "unable to perform... due to events beyond its reasonable control", while the closing proviso requires that the event render performance "impossible or unreasonably difficult"; the enumerated events are also introduced by an open "may include, but shall not be limited to". The trigger threshold and the reach of the catch-all are both uncertain.

A general cumulative-remedies clause is difficult to square with provisions 14.2 and 14.5, which fix liquidated damages "in, and only in" a stated amount as the measure of each party's exposure. Whether the University may claim other damages on top of the stipulated sum turns on that conflict.

The indemnity reaches sanctions arising from violations "of which Employee should have known and prevented" at "another NCAA member institution", an open-ended constructive-knowledge standard for pre-employment conduct. Its outer limit is not fixed by the text.
